title: Saul “reigned one year”, or was “a year old” when he began to reign?
summary: The KJV says “Saul reigned one year”. The Hebrew uses the usual formula for a king’s age at accession and reads “a son of a year was Saul in his reigning”. Brenton’s Greek Septuagint has no verse 1 at all.
text: KJV 1 Samuel 13:1: “Saul reigned one year; and when he had reigned two years over Israel,”. Hebrew (WLC): בֶּן־שָׁנָ֖ה שָׁא֣וּל בְּמָלְכֹ֑ו וּשְׁתֵּ֣י שָׁנִ֔ים מָלַ֖ךְ עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵֽל [a son of a year (was) Saul in his reigning, and two years he reigned over Israel]. Aleppo-based edition (HAC), consonants only: בן שנה שאול במלכו ושתי שנים מלך על ישראל. The same formula at 2 Samuel 2:10 (WLC): בֶּן־אַרְבָּעִ֨ים שָׁנָ֜ה אִֽישׁ־בֹּ֣שֶׁת בֶּן־שָׁא֗וּל בְּמָלְכֹו֙ עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וּשְׁתַּ֥יִם שָׁנִ֖ים מָלָ֑ךְ, which the KJV renders “was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and reigned two years”. Septuagint (Brenton Greek): the chapter page prints no verse 1; its first verse is numbered 2 and begins Καὶ ἐκλέγεται ἐαυτῷ Σαοὺλ. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/9/13/, https://bolls.life/get-text/HAC/9/13/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/2/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1SA13.htm.
reasoning: At 2 Samuel 2:10 the KJV renders the formula “son of N years … in his reigning” as the king’s age when he began to reign. At 1 Samuel 13:1 the same formula has the number “a year”, and the KJV renders it instead as a length of reign, “reigned one year”. The Hebrew as it stands gives an age, not a length of reign. The named Greek edition omits the verse.
scope: This is a finding about what the Hebrew words say, not about Saul’s real age: an age of one year cannot be meant as history, and the Hebrew text may have lost a number, but which number is not established here. The KJV wording avoids that difficulty rather than translating the formula as it does elsewhere. G is tagged only because the named Greek edition lacks the verse. KJV 1 Chronicles 20:5: “Elhanan the son of Jair slew Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite”; Hebrew (WLC): לַחְמִי֙ אֲחִי֙ גָּלְיָ֣ת הַגִּתִּ֔י [Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite]. title: David is given the shewbread, “which was not lawful for him to eat”
summary: Leviticus assigns the shewbread to Aaron and his sons. The priest at Nob gives it to David, who is not a priest, and the Gospels say David ate it and that this was not lawful. No rebuke of David or the priest for it was found.
text: KJV Leviticus 24:9: “And it shall be Aaron's and his sons'; and they shall eat it in the holy place”. KJV 1 Samuel 21:6: “So the priest gave him hallowed bread: for there was no bread there but the shewbread”. KJV Matthew 12:4: “did eat the shewbread, which was not lawful for him to eat, neither for them which were with him, but only for the priests”. Hebrew (WLC) Leviticus 24:9: וְהָֽיְתָה֙ לְאַהֲרֹ֣ן וּלְבָנָ֔יו וַאֲכָלֻ֖הוּ בְּמָקֹ֣ום קָדֹ֑שׁ [and it shall be for Aaron and for his sons, and they shall eat it in a holy place]; 1 Samuel 21:7 in the Hebrew numbering: וַיִּתֶּן־לֹ֥ו הַכֹּהֵ֖ן קֹ֑דֶשׁ [and the priest gave him holy (bread)]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/3/24/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/9/21/.
reasoning: The statute names who eats the bread. 1 Samuel narrates the priest handing it to David, and Matthew 12:4 states both that David ate it and that it was not lawful for him. David and the priest are Israelites living after Sinai. The narrator of 1 Samuel passes no judgement on the act.
scope: 1 Samuel itself narrates the giving, not the eating; the eating is stated in Matthew 12:4 and Mark 2:26. Those Gospel verses call the act unlawful but cite it in defence, not as a rebuke; whether that counts as the act being checked is left open. The priests of Nob are killed in chapter 22 on Saul’s order for helping David, which the story presents as Saul’s crime, not as punishment for the bread. No rebuke in these passages is not proof of no rebuke anywhere in the Bible: the researcher read 1 Samuel 21–22 and the three Gospel parallels and did not search every book.
